title: All the key moments from the Las Vegas Grand Prix
excerpt:
Max Verstappen claimed his fourth win of the season in Las Vegas, having withstood immense pressure throughout in a thrilling race which featured 35 changes of lead.

The frenetic pack racing produced several flashpoints, including George Russell finding the barrier late on, while Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc once again made contact.

Here are all the key moments from the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix...

Verstappen wins crazy Las Vegas GP with 35 changes of lead

Las Vegas is no stranger to staging a barnstormer of a race but this year’s event took this to another level, with a breathless Grand Prix from start to finish that featured a whopping 35 changes of lead.

Polesitter Max Verstappen made a good start to lead away, yet George Russell remained on his tail in what would prove to be a nearly race-long scrap for P1. Each time the Briton found a way past, Verstappen soon had an answer and retook the position again.

Others also got involved as the 50-lap encounter progressed, with Kimi Antonelli – who had started from P6 after a five-place grid penalty dropped him back from pole position – working his way forwards to join the fight.

While Verstappen had managed to continually find a way back into the lead throughout the race, the Red Bull driver was concerned that he might miss out on the final lap, given that he generally returned to P1 into the first corner each time rather than before the finish line.

However, Mercedes’ challenge would ultimately unravel. After being overtaken by Antonelli, Russell’s attempt to retake P2 in the latter stages backfired when he locked up and hit the barriers.

It pushed him down the order to P9, while Antonelli would go on to suffer an issue at the start of the final tour that led to him being overtaken by the McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

This gave Verstappen some breathing space for the first time all evening as he crossed the line to seal his 75th career victory and third in Las Vegas.

The four-time World Champion could barely comprehend it himself after stepping out of the car, admitting that the number of lead changes was “really, really surreal and something that I've never seen before in Formula 1 myself”.

Verstappen responds to Russell comments as rivalry reignites

The Ferraris come together again as Vasseur calls it ‘unacceptable’

The Las Vegas weekend had already posed some challenges for Ferrari before race day, with Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton ending Qualifying in P11 and P12 respectively in what Leclerc labelled as a “very poor” session.

Both drivers made progress when Saturday’s race got underway, Hamilton initially getting ahead of his team mate before the Briton fell backwards later on when he received a 10-second time penalty for leaving the track and gaining an advantage during a battle with Lando Norris.

However, in the second half of the race Hamilton was back in the top 10 and duelling with Leclerc for sixth place – only for the pair to make contact as Leclerc attempted an overtake into Turn 7, spinning Hamilton around and dropping him back to P10.

The stewards deemed Leclerc to be at fault for the incident and handed him a 10-second time penalty, leaving the Monegasque in P10 at the end of the race, while Hamilton placed in seventh.

Leclerc conceded afterwards that he would “accept the blame” given that he was handed a penalty, but admitted that he felt “quite embarrassed for the team in general” over the incident – which comes after the squad had talks in light of a clash between Leclerc and Hamilton in Mexico City.

Hamilton, meanwhile, said it was “for Ferrari to decide” if stricter rules were needed about how their drivers should race each other, while Team Principal Fred Vasseur stated that the latest incident was “unacceptable”.

“I am more than upset because that message was clear after Mexico,” Vasseur said to Sky Sports Italia. "We had a chat all together in Brazil. Today we passed the message to think about the team when they were racing together and the outcome is this one. It's mega frustrating for all of us."

Leclerc 'embarrassed' for Ferrari after Hamilton clash

Mercedes’ victory challenge falls away as Russell’s rivalry with Verstappen reignites

For much of the Las Vegas Grand Prix, Mercedes looked like they might have a victory on their hands. But after both George Russell and Kimi Antonelli spent time challenging Verstappen for the lead, the Silver Arrows ultimately left Nevada without a podium finish.

Having started alongside Verstappen on the front row, Russell was involved in a thrilling back-and-forth battle with the Red Bull driver, repeatedly snatching the lead only for the Dutchman to reclaim it moments later.

There was already plenty of tension between the pair following an FP3 incident that saw Verstappen handed a warning for erratic driving. Russell subsequently criticised his rival’s behaviour, prompting Verstappen to hit back after the race by claiming the Briton was “so far below my level”.

Back on track, Russell’s hopes unravelled when he attempted to reclaim second from Antonelli with three laps remaining, locking up at Turn 5 and hitting the barriers before recovering to finish ninth.

On the other side of the garage, Antonelli had worked his way up from sixth on the grid to challenge for victory, only for a late power issue to drop him to fourth as both McLarens swept past.

'I paid the price' - Russell laments Las Vegas GP error

McLaren secure crucial double podium in Las Vegas

Fresh from Lando Norris’ victory in Sao Paulo, McLaren had more reason to celebrate in Las Vegas as the Briton and team mate Oscar Piastri secured a double podium, giving the team a crucial boost in their battle with Red Bull for third in the teams' standings.

However, it was far from a straightforward evening for Norris, who started third but slipped as far back as P11 during a difficult opening stint as he struggled with battery deployment and straight line speed.

The Briton began making progress before the Safety Car was deployed and was running sixth by the time racing resumed, before continuing his recovery to finish second.

Piastri, meanwhile, had an even bigger mountain to climb after a 10-place grid penalty left him starting 17th. Despite losing ground during a double-stacked pit stop under the Safety Car, the Australian gained 14 places in his biggest career comeback to secure his first podium since Miami in May.

With just two rounds remaining, the result leaves McLaren only nine points behind Red Bull in the standings, with Piastri describing it as “exactly the kind of result we needed”.

F1 ACADEMY finishes with a thriller

Alisha Palmowski had already sealed the title in F1 ACADEMY, but she rounded off a terrific season with victory in the final race in Las Vegas.

The Red Bull Racing driver started on pole for Saturday’s Feature Race and battled hard with Alba Larsen as they traded places for the lead. Palmowski won for the sixth time this season, to take the title by 75 points.

“That was a really special race for me. A win in Las Vegas was on my bucket list and to secure the teams' title for Campos today makes it even more incredible,” she said afterwards.

“It wasn't a stress-free race, the slipstream effect is so big here and Alba and I were wheel to wheel throughout the race. But I managed to stay calm under the pressure and bring the victory home.”

A late Safety Car neutralised the finish, but until that point it was non-stop action up and down the field. Nina Gademan finished third as she secured second place in the standings with Alpine, while Larsen’s second place, coupled with her Reverse Grid win in Vegas, secured her fourth in the standings.

Audi’s Emma Felbermayr finished third in the championship after coming home fourth in the final race of the season.

All the stars on show in Vegas on a spectacular night of entertainment

If you wanted to see some famous faces, Las Vegas was the race to be at. The stars were out in force, with some of them even completing a lap of the track in specially designed LEGO cars.

While Hannah Waddingham, Gordan Ramsey and Terry Crews all went wheel to wheel before the race, the likes of Chris Pratt and Anthony Mackie watched on.

Keanu Reeves was given the honour of chauffeuring the top three to their post-race interviews in a special limousine, which might have been even more nerve-wracking than driving a LEGO car as the whole F1 grid watched on. Then another edition of Grid Gigs entertained the crowd, with Rei Ami headlining.

Dynamo was showing off the sort of card tricks that would not be allowed in many of the famous casinos, while F1 Ambassador Damson Idris graced the grid once again.

Sports stars were on show too, with fencer Miles Chamley-Watson and tennis player Taylor Fritz watching on, as was a certain Kim Kardashian in the Ferrari garage. And everyone watching, celebrity or fan, was certainly treated to a brilliant race in Sin City.

title: Haas confirm Camara will drive for team in final races of 2026
excerpt:
Haas have confirmed that Rafael Camara will continue to race for the team across the final two Grands Prix of the 2026 season, ahead of the Brazilian’s first full-time campaign next year.

Following Esteban Ocon’s departure ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix, reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa stepped in for that race before Camara – who was announced as one of Haas’ 2027 drivers in October – made his debut at his home event in Sao Paulo.

His second outing for the team followed in Las Vegas, but question marks had remained over whether the 21-year-old would compete for the squad in Qatar and Abu Dhabi given that this would mean abandoning his Formula 2 campaign – where he currently leads the standings.

However, it has now been announced that Camara will again get behind the wheel for Haas at the final two Grands Prix of 2026.

“We’re excited to be able to finish the season with Rafa driving and build on his first two race starts with the team in Brazil and America," said Team Principal Ayao Komatsu.

"I’m delighted that Rafa’s embraced every track session as a learning opportunity and embedded himself further within the team. We now get to finish the season together, which is advantageous to us all ahead of a relatively short off-season and as our 2027 preparations get underway.”

The confirmation comes after Camara had an eventful race of his own during his second ever Grand Prix, with the 21-year-old coming home in 16th in Las Vegas.

That was despite coming together with Sergio Perez – an incident that earned the Mexican a five-place grid drop for the next race in Qatar – with that collision triggering the Safety Car period.

Now that Camara's plans are confirmed for the rest of the year it will give the Ferrari junior more vital experience in F1 machinery as he prepares for his maiden campaign with Haas next year.

title: Wolff explains how Mercedes challenge fell apart in Vegas
excerpt:
George Russell and Kimi Antonelli both took turns to lead the Las Vegas Grand Prix, and in the closing stages both drivers were shaping up to steal victory from Max Verstappen.

However, the Mercedes challenge fell apart. With three laps to go Russell had the misfortune to lock up and slide into the barrier while, on the penultimate lap, Antonelli suffered a self-inflicted loss of battery power that allowed both McLarens to pass by.

The new World Champion crossed the line in fourth place, while Russell had to settle for P9 after reversing out of the barrier.

It was a poor reward from a race that just a few minutes earlier had promised, at the very least, a double podium finish.

“I think from George's side he made an ambitious move there on the dirty part of the track,” said team boss Toto Wolff. “And obviously he missed the braking and hit the wall, so it was an error of judgment.

“And as for Kimi, I think everything was set for an epic last lap in terms of energy deployment, and then unfortunately on the back straight, rather than passing Max, he lifted, and that caused the battery to be totally depleted. He had no energy left.

“These regs are great entertainment, and I think we saw a mega race, particularly for the Americans. I guess it was Indy 500 and NASCAR and Formula 1 mixed! I enjoyed it, but then obviously within a glimpse of a second it can be gone if you do the wrong thing.”

Expanding on what happened with Antonelli, he said: “Why we got passed is because he literally had no battery. He wanted to stay behind Max, so he lifts, he reapplies, and the battery is empty.

“And that's why even the Alpine [Pierre Gasly] almost had us, and that's why they overtook us, left, right, and centre. So that was the error. It can happen. It's complex.”

Intriguingly Wolff was confident that Antonelli could have beaten Verstappen on the crucial final lap.

“We had a last weapon up our sleeve for the final 400 metres over the left kink,” he said. “I think he would have just saved it over the line to win the race – but obviously we lost that opportunity.”

'I paid the price' – Russell laments error in Las Vegas GP

However, Wolff was happy to give credit to the man who did get it right, with Verstappen coming out on top amid relentless pressure throughout the race.

“I think Max is a deserving winner," Wolff added. "He made no mistakes, and that's why he won the race. Actually, he always had a response – some very good driving.”

Wolff is a racer at heart and, despite any frustration about the way the race finished for the Silver Arrows, he explained how he had thoroughly enjoyed it.

“You were not quite sure whether you had the position or not," he said. "The instant feedback I got from friends watching, our sponsors, was ‘that was awesome’. Stefano [Domenicali] liked it very much.

“I think that's not going to happen everywhere. In a way, it's fitting that that was the Las Vegas race, NASCAR, Indy 500, like I said, all together. To be honest, I don't know how long the race was. Ninety minutes for me, it was like 20 minutes, because it was so different, and so entertaining to watch.

“I think we were all on the edge of our seats. And I think that was a very entertaining race to watch. It was as per the rules; who manages the energy levels better? It was big slipstreams, and I find it very authentic to happen in Las Vegas like this.”

title: Racing Bulls drivers assess 'massive lost opportunity' in Vegas
excerpt:
Arvid Lindblad admits that Racing Bulls failing to score a single point in the Las Vegas Grand Prix was "a massive lost opportunity", with the Formula 1 rookie spinning out of the race behind the Safety Car.

Lindblad started from his best-ever grid position of fifth for Saturday's 50-lap race on the streets of Las Vegas, and circulated in the leading group as the racing turned into an energetic slipstreaming battle.

After a mid-race Safety Car following a collision between Sergio Perez and Rafael Camara, the entire field pitted with Lindblad rejoining in sixth.

But coming out of the penultimate corner and while attempting to warm his medium Pirelli tyres behind the Safety Car, Lindblad suffered a spin under acceleration and came to a stop broadside across the track.

Having not hit anything, Lindblad attempted to recover, glancing the wall with his right-front tyre and unable to engage reverse, before eventually retiring from the race.

"I don't know, terrible shift," said Lindblad when asked what happened. "Doesn't matter, it's my fault anyway." The rookie then shrugged when asked if cold tyres contributed to the crash before adding: "It's a massive lost opportunity."

It was a difficult day for Racing Bulls, with Liam Lawson also finishing outside the points. The New Zealander missed the start of the race as his car was still being worked on following a fuel leak.

Having entered the race a lap down, Lawson was put back on the lead lap following the Safety Car but was unable to rejoin the back of the queue in time before green flag running resumed.

It left the Kiwi P14 at the chequered flag and brought to an end a five-race run of finishing in the points.

"It's really frustrating, it's cost us points today," said Lawson on the fuel leak.

"Had a very quick car and had the potential to have a very good race but just didn't make the start and then honestly, even in the race, the Safety Car came out, I should have got my lap back.

"Sat behind the Safety Car for four laps before they let me go so I couldn't catch back up and I don't really know why. Just a frustrating day."

title: Norris reflects on 'chaotic' Las Vegas GP recovery
excerpt:
Lando Norris has described the Las Vegas Grand Prix as potentially the "most chaotic race ever in the history of Formula 1" after recovering from outside the points to claim second place and help secure a double podium for McLaren.

The Briton started third but endured a difficult opening stint, slipping as far back as P11 as he struggled with straight-line speed and battery deployment in an eventful race that saw 352 overtakes across the field.

Norris began making progress towards the end of his first stint before a mid-race Safety Car, brought out following a collision between Sergio Perez and Rafael Camara, helped him climb to P6. The McLaren driver continued his recovery after the restart, briefly taking the lead before eventually crossing the line just 0.639s behind race winner Max Verstappen, with team mate Oscar Piastri completing the podium.

"I think that must have been the most chaotic race ever in the history of Formula 1," Norris reflected. "I didn't know what was happening half the time. I didn't know if I was going to have the best race and have a chance to win or end up last.

"I had everything in this race. So it was tough. I timed things well in terms of getting back to the front. It was also a race of not making mistakes, like a lot of people made. So, a fun day. Chaotic, but a fun day, and a good result for us as a team."

Speaking in the post-race press conference, Norris explained that managing his battery deployment had been particularly challenging, leaving him vulnerable to overtakes despite having competitive pace throughout the race.

"Every time I got overtaken, I had no battery, someone else had more battery behind, and I just kept dropping back," he explained.

"The whole race was judging battery the whole time. I'm looking at the battery more than I'm looking where I'm going around this track. So it's the most important thing.

"But the second half of the race was very strong in terms of not making mistakes, staying out of the chaos of some of the others around us, and playing things right in the last three or four laps with positioning, slipstreams and battery to give myself the best chance to finish second."

The result marked Norris' seventh podium of the season and his fifth consecutive top-five finish, with the McLaren driver admitting that he had exceeded his expectations heading into the race.

"Today wasn't a race about trying to win. There was no chance we could win the race today," he said. "But P2 was the best, and we achieved it, so I'm happy."

title: Latest Hamilton-Leclerc clash ‘unacceptable’ – Vasseur
excerpt:
For Fred Vasseur and the Ferrari team, the Las Vegas Grand Prix brought a painful case of déjà vu as Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were involved in a costly tangle once more.

Just two races ago in Mexico, a first lap clash between the pair cost the Maranello team a shot at a potential victory.

That incident was followed by a summit meeting in Vasseur’s hotel room on the Thursday evening before the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, during which both drivers and their team boss aired their views.

The verdict after that gathering was that the air had been cleared and there was a new understanding between Hamilton and Leclerc. Indeed when they briefly ran together on track early in that weekend’s rain-affected race there was no issue.

In Las Vegas they both worked their way up the field after a poor qualifying session where both exited in Q2, and once again they found themselves fighting for the same piece of track for lap after lap.

Leclerc was heard asking for Hamilton to be “careful with the squeezing because it’s not going to end well,” while Lewis said, “Can you tell him to back the **** off because I’m trying to catch the guys ahead.” The team in turn urged Leclerc to be cautious with Hamilton.

However on Lap 37, everyone’s worst nightmare happened when they were battling for P6 and Leclerc knocked Hamilton into a spin, costing the latter four places.

Hamilton managed to recover to seventh by the flag, while a 10-second penalty saw Leclerc fall back to P10. It was obvious that the results could have been a lot better, but there was a much bigger picture for Vasseur.

“I don't know what could have been the outcome of the race, because it was quite difficult to imagine,” said the Frenchman afterwards. “But it's not the issue. The issue is once again it's unacceptable. It's a lack of respect for the team, for the sponsors. The same speech as after Mexico.

“I think we had a clear discussion in Sao Paulo. We passed the message to Charles during the race to think about the team when he was fighting. It's not the right word, but you can't freeze the position on this kind of race, because when you are in the slipstream, if you slow down, the guy who is behind you is overtaking you.

“And all the other teams they were able to overtake each other 20 times during the race – Antonelli/Russell, Piastri/Norris, even Isack overtook Max. Honestly, you can't imagine the frustration for me, but more important for all the guys at home.”

Leclerc ‘embarrassed’ for Ferrari as he assesses latest Hamilton clash

At the end of the race Vasseur took the unusual step of coming onto the radio and telling Leclerc that he wanted to speak to him before he attended any media activities. Asked what was discussed Vasseur made it clear that he’d voiced his opinion.

“No, it was not a discussion – I spoke!" he continued. "I think he apologised, he understands, blah blah blah. But the result is there, you do a mistake, you say my mistake, I'm sorry, but you did the mistake. Yeah, it's tough.”

He also explained that he spoke to Hamilton following the race in Nevada: “Lewis, what can he say in this kind of situation? I told him that we passed the message during the race to Charles, that he was aware.”

So is it time for Ferrari to impose different rules on the two drivers?

“Honestly, it's not a matter of rules, what you can do differently, except that you have to respect your team mate,” said Vasseur. “In this kind of race, you have to overtake the car who is in front of you. You can't stay behind. It's completely unmanageable.

“It means that you just have to do it with respect when it's your team mate, to take less risk, perhaps to come side-by-side and to come back behind.

“But you can't put it on the paper. And I think the race of today, nobody will write a scenario like this, and nobody can imagine a race like this. It means that they just have to act in a professional way.”

Asked why that wasn’t happening he added: “I think it's tension, probably the escalation of tension or whatever. It doesn't matter – it’s unacceptable.”

The obvious question from the outside is why the Sao Paulo message hadn’t got through.

“It's a good point,” said Vasseur. “It's why I want to once again have a discussion tomorrow, and also to Charles [who] will digest the situation.

"And I think it's not the right place to discuss with them two minutes after the race. I saw Charles a bit down. I told him what I have to say. I prefer to discuss with him tomorrow.”

Questions have been asked about Vasseur’s long-term relationships with both drivers, which goes back to their respective junior days, but he insisted that doesn’t compromise his role as their boss.

Hamilton frustrated by ‘really harsh’ Las Vegas penalty

“It's not because I worked with them 20 years ago or 15 years ago that it's changing my position,” he said. “It's not an issue between Lewis/Fred, or Charles/Fred. It's an issue between a team and two drivers.

“They are employees of the team, and it's not that they have a good relationship with someone. And at least I have to forget it.”

title: What the teams said – Race day in Las Vegas
excerpt:
Red Bull

Verstappen drove a masterclass in Las Vegas to record his third win here and fourth of the season. He led off the line, but was soon challenged by those behind having a tow. Despite losing the lead multiple times, every time the Dutchman kept calm and retook the place. Russell, Norris and Antonelli threw everything they could at the Red Bull man, but no one could make it stick.

Verstappen even had enough composure to debate deployment strategies with the team, worried about being passed last on the final lap and not having time to come back at his rival. But Antonelli’s late issue meant the last lap was the only one where Verstappen had some breathing room from the entire race.

As for Hadjar, his pace was very strong. He ran second and even challenged Verstappen at times. He looked on for a podium until he suffered an apparent front wing failure late on, the resultant pit stop dropping him out of the points. The Frenchman was also handed a 10-second post-race penalty for slowing down before the pit stops, as he attempted to create a gap with Red Bull double stacking their drivers.

Max Verstappen, 1st

“It was definitely one of the craziest Grands Prix I’ve ever experienced. The whole race was about managing the deployment, timing everything correctly and making sure you stayed ahead of the cars behind. They were constantly changing their strategy as well, so you always had to be aware of what was happening around you and make the right decisions. I just wanted to stay in the lead and not drop back into the pack. It was very unusual today and something completely different to what we normally experience, but the most important thing is that we won. We’ve been strong over the last few races, consistently scoring podiums, and the turnaround from the team has been very positive. We did everything right today and I’m happy we came away with the win.”

Isack Hadjar, 14th

“A disappointing end to what was a really promising first half of the race. The start was great, and it was fun to be part of what was a crazy battle. We were fighting at the front and had a lot of pace. Unfortunately, the front wing took unexpected damage and we had to box, which took us out of the fight for at least a podium. We knew we’d be fast here, and we were. The car felt so strong through the corners and, with the natural tow, we were able to keep up on the straights. It’s a shame, as everything was looking great, but that’s racing sometimes.”

Laurent Mekies, Team Principal

“What an incredible race and an outstanding performance from Max and the entire Team. We knew that energy management and the slipstream would play a significant role today, but I don't think anyone anticipated quite so much overtaking. Max was simply exceptional, both in attack and defence, keeping his composure right until the very last lap. The communication between Max, his engineers and the pit wall was outstanding, and that teamwork made a real difference in such an unpredictable race.

"At the same time, it is a real shame for Isack. He had fantastic pace, was right up there with Max and at one stage we were running P1 and P2. He deserved so much more from this weekend, and we owe him an apology for what happened today. we will analyse what happened with his front wing and come back stronger in Doha.

"We started the weekend on the back foot, but the way everyone responded, took risks and worked together to turn things around was remarkable. This victory is another fantastic reward for the hard work of everyone in the Team.

"We will enjoy the moment tonight, but then our focus will turn to the last two races of the season and trying to perform at that level again there.”

McLaren

Norris started from P3, but he struggled on the soft tyres and dropped all the way out of the top 10 in the first stint. Piastri was going better on the mediums and soon climbed back into the top 10 and was even running ahead of his team mate at times. Somehow despite multiple moves, those two kept their battles clean.

The Australian lost out in the double stack behind the Safety Car, but soon climbed back to where his team mate was running. On the mediums, they looked much more competitive and weaved their way forward, with Norris even picking off Russell and Verstappen and leading for a few corners at one point.

They were behind the two Mercedes cars when Russell ran off, and both picked off Antonelli right at the end to score what, at times this weekend, looked a very unlikely double podium.

Lando Norris, 2nd

“It was a chaotic race from start to finish, and every lap brought something to manage: battery use, positioning, slipstreams and whether to attack or defend. I was down the order early on, and it took time to understand how to use the battery and get the most from the car. Once we worked that out, we started making progress. The cornering speed was strong, but our lack of straight-line speed made it difficult to move forward and hold position. We timed the opportunities well, especially in the closing laps, and second place was the best we could achieve. I’m very happy for the team to come away with a double podium.

“We weren’t expecting this result, particularly at a circuit where we knew we might struggle. The team did a great job, and we’re making progress, but there is still plenty we want to improve. Qatar will be a very different challenge, so we’ll keep working, stay reasonably optimistic and see where we are when we get there.”

Oscar Piastri, 3rd

“I am very happy to be back on the podium, especially on a day where we weren't expecting it. It's a great result for the team and to have both Lando and I on the podium, making up 14 positions on my side, is exactly what we needed.

“We were able to maximise across a lot of different aspects to be able to put it all together. We were able to get through the pack well both times, and the overtaking was good fun. While we have work to do on it, our straight-line speed felt okay, especially with the power of the slipstream, and our overall pace was good. Our strength in the corners meant we were able to close up there, which was positive.

“For the final two races, we hope to be quick and to keep working at the points gap to Red Bull. Thank you to the team for their work so far. Today felt like a step in the right direction, and while it was a unique race on a very different circuit, let's see if we can carry this strong momentum into the final two races of the season.”

Andrea Stella, Team Principal

“What a race! Las Vegas treated all Formula 1 fans to an incredible spectacle: 50 laps of thrills and overtaking manoeuvres that will go down in the history of the sport and represent the best possible promotion for Formula 1 in the US.

“For us, there is also the double joy of seeing both our drivers on the podium and of being the team that scored the most points on a circuit where our car was clearly not competitive enough to achieve such a result. This is the result of the work done first and foremost by Lando and Oscar, who probably delivered one of the best races of their careers. The support they received from their respective engineering teams, assisted by the HPP staff, was also crucial: finding the best way to manage energy and slipstream today was truly complicated, especially in a race that offered not a moment’s respite from the start right through to the chequered flag.

“Lando managed to find the right solutions to fight his way back after an early stage in which he paid dearly for the MCL40’s lack of top speed on this circuit. Oscar staged a superb comeback from 17th on the starting grid, and the podium is a fitting reward for a performance of the very highest standard. I was particularly pleased to see how both of them battled it out at various stages of the race, whilst bearing in mind that the team’s interests are always the priority.

“With this result, we’ve managed to close the gap on Red Bull: nine points separate us with two races still to go. Now we must prepare as best we can for the final rounds, first in Qatar and then in Abu Dhabi, where we believe the MCL40 – thanks in part to the updates we introduced between São Paulo and Las Vegas – can be competitive and allow Lando and Oscar to fight for victory once again.”

Mercedes

A case of what might have been for Mercedes. Russell was the first on the attack, repeatedly passing Verstappen for the lead only to lose out a few corners later. Meanwhile, while he was battling for first, occasionally losing second and fighting with Hadjar for good measure, Antonelli was climbing back through the field. He was the only front runner to start on the mediums, which hampered him off the line.

On the softs late on Antonelli was able to pass the two McLaren cars and Gasly to run third, and then he picked off his team mate. He took his turn passing Verstappen for the lead, only to be re-passed a few corners later. But there was a late sting in the tail as Russell made a move on Antonelli on the penultimate lap, locked up and hit the barriers which dropped him from P3 to ninth. Then on the last lap, Antonelli played with his deployment to make sure he had battery to attack Verstappen through the last few corners.

Instead, that left him with no battery and he was picked off by both McLaren cars to drop off the podium, the Italian doing well to hold Gasly at bay and stay in fourth.

Kimi Antonelli, 4th

"That was a really unusual and exciting race, although obviously it is frustrating to finish the way we did. We were in the fight for the win throughout and, going into the final lap, I wanted to stay behind Max (Verstappen) and keep the overtake mode available to give myself the best possible opportunity on the final straights. I lifted to try to achieve that, but unfortunately it compromised the battery deployment, and I came out of the chicane with almost no energy. That meant I couldn’t attack him and we also lost the podium.

"It was disappointing because I genuinely felt we had a chance to win today. Before that, though, there were plenty of positives. There was so much back and forth racing, and you had to be very strategic with your positioning and energy management. I learned a lot from the race and also from these conditions, where I know I still have room to improve. We have two races left and we want to continue to fight for wins and finish the season strongly."

George Russell, 9th

"That was an incredibly unusual race and obviously I’m disappointed with how mine ended. The slipstream was massive and the different energy management strategies meant the order was constantly changing. With a few laps to go, I knew that if I wanted to fight Max (Verstappen) for the win, I needed to be P2 going on to the final lap. I saw the opportunity to pass Kimi, went for it, but unfortunately got it slightly wrong, locked up and paid the price. I’m not happy with the outcome, but I don’t regret going for the move. I could have been conservative and probably come home in P3, but at this stage of the season I want to fight for victories. It didn’t work out today, but at least we went for it."

Toto Wolff, Head of Mercedes-Benz Motorsport

"That was a fittingly thrilling Grand Prix for Las Vegas; crazy place, crazy race! We were in the fight throughout but are naturally disappointed with our result. Even when you have won both championships, you are never completely satisfied in motor racing. You still want to win every race, and today we had the opportunity to achieve more than we ultimately did.

"For George, he was looking to make the pass into Turn 5, got onto the dirty part of the track under braking and couldn’t make the move stick. That ended his chance of battling for the win. Meanwhile Kimi was trying to manage his positioning behind Max (Verstappen) ahead of the final lap, but the lift and subsequent reapplication of the throttle cost him energy deployment and, ultimately, the chance to fight to the line and his place on the podium.

"Those are small margins, but against this level of competition they make the difference. With such low degradation, there wasn’t a significant performance offset between the cars, so it became a really interesting race about positioning, judgement and race craft. We can appreciate the spectacle while still being frustrated with our own race. We know we could have done a better job today and we will look at those moments, learn from them and aim to finish the final two races of the season more strongly than we did today."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"It's obviously disappointing to be running P2 and P3 with three laps to go, feeling like we had a shot at the win, to ultimately cross the line P4 and P9. It was an unusual Grand Prix from a racing point of view. Getting yourself in front was relatively straightforward, but staying there was the difficult bit. The combined effect of the tow and overtake mode made it almost impossible for anyone to break away, so much of the afternoon was spent in the bunch, jockeying for position.

"Kimi did a good job of steadily moving forward while George was busy racing Verstappen. The Safety Car came at a point that took away much of the strategic variation, so from there it became a question of how cleverly you could manage and deploy your energy. We didn't have a great balance with either car, at different points lacking front and rear grip. That meant we were losing ground through the corners and having to spend more energy to recover it on the straights.

"Going into the final laps, we were looking forward to an exciting finish. Unfortunately, George dropped out of contention when he out-braked himself into T5 and tapped the wall. Kimi meanwhile lifted into T14 to stay behind and retain overtake mode. That affected his harvesting through the final corner sequence and left him with no energy to defend from the two McLarens.

"We didn't need a reminder that we have plenty of work to do if we want to defend both championships next year, but we got one today. We'll be working flat out to maximise the final two races, but more importantly to learn everything we can from them and make sure we put ourselves in the strongest possible position for 2027."

Alpine

The Alpine had very good pace in Las Vegas, which was not a surprise considering how well they went in Monza. Gasly fought his way forward and was running third after the Safety Car period, but was told to nurse his car which was overheating.

That was a shame for the Frenchman, but he still managed to finish a very strong P5 which is his best result of the season. Colapinto matched his best result with sixth, after a decent race where he kept out of trouble, pulled off a number of good moves and was fighting wheel to wheel with the McLaren and Ferrari cars on merit.

Pierre Gasly, 5th

“That was an enjoyable race and finishing P5 and P6 as a team is a very good result. I honestly feel like we could have been on the podium but we had to turn the power down throughout the race to manage our engine temperatures so we need to review why that was and what we can do better next time. It was basically a slipstream game, so it meant following closely the cars ahead to stay in the fight. I know it was tough for the team to be on top of a lot of things and everyone did a great job – from strategy to the engineers and the pit crew for a good pit-stop – it was all very well managed. It was a busy one for me at the wheel – focusing on attacking the car ahead while keeping an eye on the car behind as well as doing all the switch changes, there really was a lot going on. We are very pleased with the result and battling with Red Bull, McLaren, Mercedes and Ferrari throughout the race was very fun and hopefully next season we can do more of that!”

Franco Colapinto, 6th

“It was a race right up until the chequered flag and was a lot of fun, even more so when you have a result like that and score points for the team. Generally, I'm very happy with how the race went and with the final result, equalling my best-ever finish in Formula One. We have been competitive all weekend here, so to come away with 18 points is a great reward for our efforts. It's good to have two cars up there and fighting with the top four teams, which we don't do every weekend. Naturally, when you're in the mix, you also want a bit more, but that's a good feeling to have as you're never fully satisfied and shows we were competitive this weekend. It was fun behind the wheel and probably fun to watch also on TV and in the stands, but it was also quite strategic with using the tow, managing energy levels and temperatures. I'm happy for the whole team at Enstone for this result, which they deserve especially after the difficulties we've had in recent races.”

Flavio Briatore, Executive Advisor

“It was a fantastic team result today, and both Pierre and Franco did a super job and drove well in a race that required a lot of precision and concentration. The racing was close and exciting which was great for Formula One. This result gives us a lot to be optimistic about and also gives the team something to celebrate at Enstone after a tough run of results in the second half of the season. Overall, it has been a very strong weekend for the whole team in Las Vegas and, with 18 points scored, it is also our best result so far this season. So well done to the whole team.”

Ferrari

Ferrari leave Las Vegas with another headache to sort. The race was going surprisingly well for them after their struggles in Qualifying, with Hamilton climbing back through the field and passing his team mate cleanly. But he was handed a 10-second time penalty for overtaking Norris off track. When everyone pitted under the Safety Car, he was left out – had he come in for tyres and to serve the penalty, the double stack would have hampered Leclerc.

Hamilton therefore dropped to P14 when he did pit next time around, and sounded suitably frustrated by the turn of events. But he soon recovered back to where his team mate was running. Hamilton again passed Leclerc, but late on the Monegasque tried to retake the place and the two made contact. Hamilton came off worse, spinning as he dropped to P10. He recovered a couple of places, while Leclerc finished sixth on the road – but he was blamed for the incident by the stewards and had a 10-second time penalty applied when he crossed the line.

And based on Leclerc’s radio post-race, the team were not too happy with the move from the Monegasque driver.

Lewis Hamilton, 7th

"The team did a great job with the strategy and we had strong race pace. I’m proud of everyone in the garage and my engineers for all their hard work.

"I felt a podium was on today but it was a tough race and the penalty, followed by the contact, made that difficult. I kept my head down and kept pushing and we fought our way back into the battle. There are positives to take from today, even if the result doesn’t fully reflect what I think it could have been."

Charles Leclerc, 10th

"The race didn’t finish well for us, and my mistake was part of that. I accept the penalty and we will review what I could have done differently so it doesn’t happen again. I’m sorry for the team, for everyone in Maranello and for the points we lost today."

Fred Vasseur, Team Principal

"For the second time in three races, something unacceptable has happened between our drivers, and this cannot continue. We sent a very clear message to both drivers in Brazil, and today during the race we told them to think about the team when racing each other. Of course, in this kind of race you cannot freeze the positions because, with the slipstream, if you slow down, the car behind will overtake you. But our drivers should have handled the situation differently, as other teammates did both in front of and behind them. Charles knows he made a mistake and apologised, but that doesn’t change the result.

"It’s difficult to put into words how frustrating today’s episode is for the whole team. The pace was good and the podium was not out of reach. Once again, what happened shows a lack of respect for the team, for everyone working at the track and back in Maranello, and for all our partners. We will discuss what happened internally in the coming days."

Williams

Williams expected to go okay here relatively speaking, and so it proved for Sainz. He made some moves in the first stint, but emerged from the pit stops in the top 10 thanks to a few rivals losing out having to double stack. Sainz did not have to do so given his team mate was not even in the race – overheating brakes on the grid meaning the unlucky Albon did not even take the start.

Sainz then ran in the top 10 for the rest of the race, losing a couple of positions but then inheriting P8 courtesy of Russell’s late mistake, and Leclerc’s time penalty. Eighth is Sainz’s best result of the year and the team’s first points since Baku.

Carlos Sainz, 8th

“I’m very happy and proud of our performance today! P8 might not seem much, but we delivered on track and executed a flawless race. I did the best start of the season and we took every chance that was available to us, making sure to save my battery when it mattered, which helped me overtake George over the line for P8. It was consistent qualifying laps for the whole race, so I’m glad it paid off and we could bring home some points for the team after a long season."

Alex Albon, DNS

“It was a frustrating weekend, and obviously disappointing not to get to race here in Las Vegas. We had a brake overheating issue on laps to grid that caused too much damage for us to race. We'll investigate further to fully understand what happened.

"Carlos had a great drive, and it's nice to see the team in the points today. Looking ahead, we'll regroup and head to Qatar focused on making the most of the weekend."

James Vowles, Team Principal

“What an exciting finish to this Grand Prix. It is always spectacular here and today if you could stay in the tow everything was possible. Well done to Carlos, he managed the last few laps perfectly and executed a really great manouvre to keep energy to cross the line into a brilliant P8. For Alex, unfortunately it was over before it started. He was warming the brakes on the laps to grid and the rears caught fire – when they did, they burned the safety tethers which stop the wheels coming away from the car in an accident. Once those are damaged it means a complete suspension change, and we simply couldn’t do that before the race started. It was a travesty, because I know Alex would have been competitive today. It was great to see Carlos able to fight for points on merit and that is what we're pushing for next year, using Qatar and Abu Dhabi to keep learning for the future."

Audi

Audi did not manage to finish in the points in Las Vegas, coming close yet again but with no joy. Nonetheless, both drivers fought hard and were in the thick of the action. However, they will not be too happy with having a car finish 11th for the 11th time this season.

They did have a fun fight with the Haas cars, Bortoleto managing to just about keep rival Bearman at bay. But the team are running out of time to catch Haas in the standings, remaining three points adrift with two rounds remaining.

Nico Hulkenberg, 11th

“It was a bit of a mixed race today. We had some good fighting after the Safety Car, especially with Gabi and Ollie, which was fun. The rest of the race was fairly quiet for me. Once you lose the tow around here, you give away so much lap time on the straights, which makes it difficult to recover. I think that was pretty much the maximum we could do today.

“Energy management was a bit of a curveball and felt like a moving target at times, so there's certainly plenty for us to understand and take away from this race. It's all valuable experience for us as a team, and we'll have a good look at everything to see how we can improve.”

Gabriel Bortoleto, 12th

“It was an eventful race in terms of overtakes and how much was happening, but overall, it wasn’t the easiest for us. We have struggled with issues on my car throughout the weekend, and I am disappointed because at one point I was up to P8 and really thought I could stay in the points. Unfortunately, it was difficult to keep up with the cars around me, but I gave my best and I think we did everything we could today. Now, I want to move forward and focus on the last two races of the year. Hopefully, we can have a couple of clean weekends and bring home some points.”

Allan McNish, Racing Director

“Formula One put on a fantastic show tonight. With plenty of overtaking and action throughout the field, the fans certainly got a taste of what Las Vegas is all about.

“On our side, we finished P11 and P12. We knew it was going to be a tough race, and it was certainly full of action for us as well. We showed good performance at different stages of the race, but unfortunately, with the way the positions changed after the Safety Car restart, we lost some ground and weren't able to get back into the leading group, which had pulled away together due to the very powerful tow you get on this circuit.

“Both Nico and Gabi had tremendous battles with Ollie Bearman and the Haas throughout the race, with plenty of intense moments and some very close racing. Ultimately, we came very close, but finished just short of the points. Now we move on to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, and the fight is very much still on.”

Haas

Bearman was always up against it from the back of the grid, and opted to start on the mediums. That left him on the faster soft tyres for the second stint, which enabled the Haas man to climb up the order. As for Camara, he was running well until a collision with Perez. The Cadillac tried to overtake down the inside, Camara turned in and the two collided.

The rookie was spun into the barriers but managed to continue, limping back to the pits but coming back out to finish the race. The stewards investigated that collision, and found the Cadillac man at fault.

Oliver Bearman, 13th

“I had a good first lap and had a lot of fun fighting with the Audis. I had some good battles with Nico and Gabi in that second stint. It was definitely one of the more interesting races of the year, it went by very quickly as we were all fighting so hard. At one point, I was in front of both of them, but that didn’t last very long. Before the race, with the team, we said we should finish P14, and we finished P13, so that’s a win in my book, but unfortunately we’re not quick enough to score points on merit. We have to keep fighting them and slow them down a little, and I tried my best to do that.”

Rafael Camara, 16th

“Some parts of the race were quite fun. We had some overtakes and it’s always good to be battling, but towards the end, it was a bit more boring being alone, then I got overtaken by Hadjar and Lawson. I think overall it was a positive race and throughout I was improving. At the start, it was a bit hard to get temperature into the tyres and get a good first lap, but once we had everything under control, it was a decent race. There was a touch with Checo, but we need to review that. It’s very rare to get laps in before your first full season in Formula 1, and this weekend has been very useful.”

Ayao Komatsu, Team Principal

“Our drivers did a good job today. Ollie fought with the Audis until the very last lap, so that’s everything we had. With Rafa, we need to improve the starts, but it was a huge improvement from Brazil in terms of consistency and he’s learning so fast. Of course, here, the tow matters so much and with Rafa being in free air, his lap times don’t look that good, but in corners, his performance was very good. I’m really happy with both drivers. In Qatar, it’s going to be a very different challenge, but we’re going to give it our best shot.”

Racing Bulls

With two cars starting solidly in the top 10, this should have been a night to remember for Racing Bulls. Instead, it soon became a night to forget, with Lawson unable to take the start after a fuel leak was detected. He did eventually start, one lap down and thus was never in contention for the top 10. Lindblad though started very, very strongly and kept pace with the front runners. He looked on for a really big haul of points, but after pitting behind the Safety Car, the rookie lit up his medium tyres.

That sent him into a spin and ended his race, and to add insult to injury, the team’s biggest rivals Alpine managed to score with both cars. Racing Bulls still have a decent lead in the fight for P5 in the Teams’ Championship, but another result like this and suddenly that lead won’t look so comfortable.

Liam Lawson, 15th

"A very tough day today. We’ve had a really fast race car all weekend, so it’s disappointing that a fuel leak before the race meant we couldn’t make the start. The guys and girls did a fantastic job to fix the car and get everything back together, and even more impressively, get me out on track without any further issues. Starting a lap down meant we were never really able to get back into the fight, so it ended up being quite a lonely race. There are plenty of positives to take away from this weekend and carry into the final two races. We’ll keep pushing and look to come away with some more points."

Arvid Lindblad, DNF

"It’s really disappointing to end our race this way. Up until that moment, we were having an amazing battle with the top teams, which is something I hadn’t really experienced before in Formula 1. I’m still struggling to understand exactly what happened; I was warming up the tyres when the Safety Car was out and as soon as I got on the throttle, the car just spun. Ultimately, it was my fault and I sincerely apologise to the team, as it was a huge opportunity lost. We’ll analyse what happened and learn from it. For now, our focus shifts to the remaining races of this last triple-header of the season."

Alan Permane, Team Principal

"First of all, we apologise to Liam for not giving him a car to start the race from the grid today. We had a fuel leak which was complicated to fix, but the mechanics did a great job to get it out when they did. Arvid unfortunately had a difficult race after losing control of the car under the Safety Car. We’ll need to look closely at the gear shift to understand whether that may have contributed, but there’s no doubt he had the pace today and was capable of racing with the top four.

"We’ll put this one behind us and head to Qatar in full attack mode. We’re confident the car will be competitive there, and we’re looking forward to putting together a strong weekend as we enter the final two races of the season."

Aston Martin

Aston Martin expected to struggle in Las Vegas, the long straight punishing their car. As such, neither driver was able to climb up the order despite the chaotic racing. Alonso wound up not finishing the race, although as he retired so late, he was classified as P19. Stroll at least did see the flag, the first time he has finished a race since Austin.

Fernando Alonso, DNF

“We were lacking any straight-line performance tonight as we have all weekend. I was trying to follow the train of cars ahead, but with the lack of power, it wasn't possible to move forward and very difficult to defend. We were making up time in the corners but then losing more than two seconds a lap on the straights with this power unit. I then retired the car just before the end because it felt like we had a PU issue. We go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi next and will look to do our best for the final two rounds.”

Lance Stroll, 17th

“I was battling with Valtteri and Fernando and it felt like our own race at the back. We have no performance in the power unit, so we always knew Las Vegas would be tough for us and there’s not much to take away from this weekend. We made it to the finish so that’s a positive, but we still had the same issues we've had all year. We are missing around two seconds in our straight line speed, so Honda need to find more power."

Mike Krack, Chief Trackside Officer

“Our fight today was with Cadillac and we ended the race ahead of Bottas with Lance in P17. Given our pace and lack of straight line performance, that was the most we could achieve. Fernando was racing with Lance all afternoon, back and forth, but he stopped the car on the final lap because he felt there was an engine issue. Both cars ran the same strategy of Soft and Medium, pitting under the Safety Car. There was not much for us to fight for this weekend but hopefully we can be more competitive next week in Qatar.”

Cadillac

Cadillac were having some fun on home soil, but as Perez spied a gap and made a move when fighting Camara, it all went wrong. The gap closed as the Mexican tried to dive down the inside, and the two made contact. The collision saw Perez then hit the barriers and immediately retire, which brought out the Safety Car. The stewards declared Perez at fault, and handed him a five-place grid drop for the next event.

As for Bottas, he came home in P18 after pitting twice, unable to keep Camara behind in the closing stages.

Sergio Perez, DNF

“We had good pace and were fighting with the cars around us, which was positive. It was a good opportunity to try and make something happen and fight our way forward. Unfortunately, I then had an incident. I was alongside him (Camara) and expected him to leave me enough room to make the corner. I was planning to make the move afterwards, into Turn 16, but unfortunately he didn’t see me.

“By the time I tried to avoid him, it was already too late. He apologised afterwards and explained that he simply hadn’t seen me. It’s frustrating, because we were having a good race and fighting with other cars. We were making progress as a team, but unfortunately the incident made things a little more difficult. It is what it is, we move forward.”

Valtteri Bottas, 18th

“There was lots of action, which is nice! It’s good to be there fighting. Today the strategy was good, both pit stops were good and we finished the race, so lots of positives to take away. We’re at the stage now that we know we’re lacking pace but we know that next year can be very different. It was fun, on this track there are so many opportunities to overtake which makes a big difference. It’s good to finish the race, we got good mileage and hopefully we can keep this momentum for the last two races this season.”

Marcin Budkowski, Team Principal

“A contrasting night for the team. It was an action packed race and Valtteri brought it home after a long battle with the Aston Martins. During the Safety Car we elected to stop on consecutive laps to get back on our preferred soft tyre. The team also executed two great pitstops. After a tough few races for Valtteri I am pleased he took the chequered flag.

“For Checo it was an unfortunate incident with Camara, which is frustrating, both for Checo and the team, but it happens when you race hard with other drivers. Now the team has an epic journey to Qatar. For the trackside team and those supporting remotely this is a huge undertaking, so we will endeavor to recover quickly and focus on the job ahead. It is important to keep our focus as a team and use the final two races to learn for next season.”

title: Hadjar 'clueless' on reason for front wing failure in Vegas
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar conceded he was still "waiting for the team to tell me what happened" after his front wing broke during the Las Vegas Grand Prix, denying the Red Bull driver a chance of a podium.

The Frenchman featured in the lead battle during the early stages of the 50-lap race on the streets of Las Vegas, moving up from his starting position of P4 to challenge Red Bull team mate Max Verstappen for the lead.

After a mid-race pit stop under the Safety Car, Hadjar rejoined in third and immediately looked to challenge George Russell's Mercedes at the restart, only for the front wing on his car to collapse on the approach to Turn 5.

"I'm waiting for the team to tell me what happened at the moment. I just am clueless," said Hadjar.

"I actually didn't touch anything and the car just broke, so at the moment I'm just really curious. I know there was a massive bump on the track.

"I was braking, maybe that's what caused the issue but I don't really know now. But anyway, I had fun up to that point."

After pitting for a new front wing, Hadjar circulated towards the back of the field before eventually crossing the line in P14, only to drop a further position after receiving a 10-second penalty post-race.

This was after Hadjar had backed the pack up when the Safety Car was deployed in order to create a gap to Verstappen ahead as both drivers headed for the pits.

The stewards noted that "Car 6 significantly reduced its speed, at one point travelling approximately 100 km/h slower than Car 3, which was ahead of it".

The document added: "The Stewards considered that Car 6 was driving unnecessarily slowly for tactical reasons and that such conduct constituted a breach of the applicable regulations."

title: Oscar Piastri ends long F1 podium drought after bizarre Las Vegas chaos
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri returned to the F1 podium for the first time in six months after a chaotic Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Starting 17th after a 10-place grid drop for an engine change, Piastri was able to capitalise on the strong yo-yo racing slipstream effect to climb up the order and duel with the likes of George Russell, Kimi Antonelli, Pierre Gasly, and team-mate Lando Norris.

In the end, Norris got ahead to finish second, but Piastri was third over the line for his first F1 podium finish since third in May's Miami Grand Prix, 18 races ago.

It is his best finish since fourth in the Austrian GP in June after a tough run for the Australian - who also ended the longest podium drought of his career.

Reflecting, Piastri spoke of the chaos as cars used the slipstream effect to continually pass and repass rivals.

"They say Las Vegas is the entertainment capital of the world, and I think that was pretty entertaining to be part of," he said.

"Obviously, starting from the back, I didn't know how it was going to go, and we could make progress pretty quickly, and I could kind of work out pretty early on that it was just staying as one massive pack.

"So yeah, the double stack and the pit stop was a bit of a shame, but it didn't really matter in the end. I mean, everyone was just in such a big pack, and it was bizarre to be a part of.

"It was pretty random. You would pass somebody on one straight super easy, and then the next straight you would struggle, and then with someone else, it would be different straights where you had strengths and weaknesses. So it was a little bit random.

"And every time you caught the back of the train, or you overtook someone, you thought you were going to win the race by 10 seconds, but then you'd get ahead and suddenly realise that the slipstream was doing a lot of the work.

"So a crazy race, but happy to be back on the podium."

title: Liam Lawson ends 52-year F1 wait despite Las Vegas GP misery
excerpt:
Liam Lawson set the first fastest lap by a New Zealander in F1 since 1974 in a Las Vegas Grand Prix he almost did not start.

Just prior to the race, where he was due to start in seventh place, Lawson's Racing Bulls machine developed a fuel leak and was wheeled back into the garage for repairs - with the team able to get him back on track, having lost just one lap.

However, running by himself, Lawson was unable to latch onto the field in the slipstream-fest and had an otherwise lonely race, although he was joined briefly by Isack Hadjar's Red Bull after the front-wing failure required a new nose for the Red Bull.

Ultimately, Lawson finished in 15th on the road, but Hadjar was handed a 10-second time penalty for slowing down too much and holding up George Russell during the entry into the pit-lane, with Lawson promoted to 14th.

He had been just 0.100s behind Hadjar on the run to the line, with this tow aiding Lawson in setting the fastest lap of the race, a 1:35.591.

It is the fastest lap of Lawson's career, as he became the 142nd driver to set one, and the first for a New Zealander since Denny Hulme at the 1974 Belgian GP.

Overall, it is the 16th fastest lap by a New Zealander, and the first for Racing Bulls as a constructor, as it became the 46th squad to do so.

Reflecting on his evening, Lawson praised the team for its efforts in ensuring he had a quick machine after the fuel leak.

"I mean, that is really the big question," Lawson replied when asked by media, including RacingNews365, about when the fuel leak developed.

"What we need to answer is what we can do in the future to figure it out earlier, and we actually had a similar thing happen in Monaco this year - and both times the guys and girls have done a really, really good job to put the car together and maximise.

"For us to go out on track today and have absolutely no issue and have a really fast race car is massively impressive from everybody, and I just feel from them that I couldn't deliver because we lost a lap."

After the mid-race safety car, Lawson was allowed to unlap himself, but was not immediately released, meaning he could not catch the back of the pack for the restart.

[Article continues below]

Safety car confusion

Although he did earn the lap back under the safety car, Lawson was not able to latch onto the back of the pack for the restart as it took four laps to release him - something he expressed confusion at.

"I got it back, and we actually probably could have still had a really good race," he said.

"But I don't know why they took four laps to release me.

"I get that when there are marshals on the track, and there is safety around it; I can understand that, but it is still a double yellow.

"I can still slow for the double yellow zone and follow a delta; there is nothing stopping me. I'm not going to blow through that zone at high speed, but it means I can do the whole lap and catch back up.

"Unfortunately, they waited four laps, and then they gave me half a lap to catch back up, and I restarted 25 seconds behind the field."

title: Significant F1 record shattered during chaotic Las Vegas Grand Prix
excerpt:
Formula 1's 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix produced 352 overtakes, smashing the previous record of 186 set at the 2023 Dutch Grand Prix, as Max Verstappen held off a chasing pack to win his 75th race.

The surge in passing stemmed directly from this year's technical regulations overhaul.

Active straight-line aerodynamics, combined with varying hybrid battery deployment, created closing speed deltas of 20 to 30 km/h on the approach to braking zones, turning the long Strip straight and the final corner into a rolling slipstream battle all race long.

Las Vegas' layout compounded the effect, as with no high-speed corners to let leaders break clear, the field ran as a tightly bunched pack rather than strung out, with low tyre degradation on the smooth surface allowing cars to follow nose-to-tail lap after lap without the usual thermal penalty.

Track temperatures around 12 degrees Celsius produced minimal graining on the soft and medium compounds, further preserving pace through the stints.

A Safety Car on lap 19 then squeezed the majority of the field onto a matching one-stop strategy, keeping the pack compressed through the second half of the race and fuelling the yo-yo position swaps that followed, with 35 of the overtakes coming for the race lead alone.

Verstappen was a consistent challenger at the front and faced challenges from a variety of drivers, including his team-mate Isack Hadjar.

Lando Norris, who finished second for McLaren, acknowledged afterwards that the scale of the electrical boost made some passes feel almost too easy and that they did not feel like true overtakes.

title: Why latest Ferrari turmoil adds significant fuel to Leclerc-Hamilton soap opera
excerpt:
Despite a meeting post-Mexico City, Ferrari's drivers clashed yet again in Las Vegas. Just what has happened between the two this year?

Under the neon glow of the Las Vegas Strip, Ferrari's season-long soap opera found its latest, and most costly, chapter.

Charles Leclerc was been handed a 10-second time penalty after spinning team-mate Lewis Hamilton out of position during the Las Vegas Grand Prix, the third time this season the Ferrari pair have come to blows on track.

What began as a straightforward fight for position on lap 38 has instead reignited questions that have followed Ferrari all year: can two title-calibre drivers coexist without a formal pecking order, and how much longer can Maranello afford to find out the hard way?

The incident occurred at Turn 7, when Leclerc attempted an inside move on Hamilton and made contact with the Briton's rear-left corner, sending him into a spin.

Stewards ruled Leclerc had attacked from too far back and had not earned the right to the corner, finding him wholly to blame for the collision. The penalty dropped Leclerc from sixth on the road to 10th in the final classification, while Hamilton recovered from the spin to finish seventh.

Team principal Fred Vasseur called the clash unprofessional and "unacceptable", pointing out that Leclerc had ignored direct pit-wall instructions to back off and prioritise the team.

Vasseur summoned Leclerc over the radio immediately after the chequered flag for a debrief, with further internal discussions scheduled for Sunday morning. It was a strikingly public rebuke from a team principal who, for much of the year, had preferred to let his drivers race.

Las Vegas was not an isolated flashpoint, but rather the latest instalment in a feud that has simmered since the European summer.

At Monza in September, Leclerc crowded Hamilton wide on the opening lap before crashing out himself on the next tour.

Hamilton later pushed publicly for Ferrari to introduce written rules of engagement for wheel-to-wheel battles with his team-mate, drawing a contrast with the framework he had grown used to at Mercedes.

Vasseur rejected the idea, arguing that rigid guidelines do not work in modern pack racing and that mutual respect between drivers should be enough, an equal-opportunity approach he maintained even as the collisions mounted.

The pair then clashed again at the Mexico City Grand Prix, where both Ferraris ran off circuit while fighting for position. Leclerc received a five-second penalty for gaining an advantage by leaving the track.

That incident prompted Vasseur to hold clear-the-air meetings in Sao Paulo, stressing that the team and brand had to come before the rivalry between his two drivers.

Unlike Mexico City and Monza, where neither driver faced sporting sanction, Las Vegas produced a public rebuke from Vasseur himself, a marked escalation in both the stakes and the scrutiny.

It remains unclear whether Ferrari will now move to impose binding team orders or a formal driver hierarchy for the final two rounds of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, a question the Maranello outfit has so far left unanswered through successive rounds of internal talks.

For a team that has spent all year insisting its drivers can be trusted to race each other fairly, the Las Vegas desert may finally have forced a reckoning.

title: McLaren make stunning claim in high praise for Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri
excerpt:
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella believes the Las Vegas Grand Prix was Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri's best as team-mates; such was the level of cooperation and teamwork between them.

They started the 50-lap race at diverging ends of the grid, with Norris lining up third and Piastri down in P17 after a 10-place penalty for a power unit change.

However, as the evening in Sin City progressed, they converged at the lower reaches of the points. The former was suffering due to the MCL40's lack of straight-line speed and short gear ratios, whilst the car was a strong-enough platform to help the latter move forward.

From there, they adopted a collaborative approach to work forward, taking advantage of the close-quarters yo-yo racing by picking off rivals systematically and getting themselves in position to capitalise on the chaos ahead.

At the start of Lap 48, they were running fourth and fifth, only for George Russell to put his Mercedes in the wall and Kimi Antonelli to make an energy management error, leaving the door wide open for an unexpected podium, with Norris leading home Piastri.

Speaking to media, including RacingNews365, after the race, Stella detailed just how effective — and clever — the pair had been.

"In terms of drivers, let me say that I think for both Oscar and Lando, this is one of their best races," the McLaren boss said. "Because the ratio between the outcome, what they were able to extract in terms of result, and what the team made available in terms of potential of the car, I think is one of the best for both.

"I was very concerned about our raceability, a combination of the top speed and the [gear] ratios, and somehow Lando and Oscar figured out how to use even the slipstream.

"And when, for other cars, it would have been okay to move away from the slipstream and complete an overtake, they realised, 'don't do it', because we are not even going to be able to overtake.

"So there was a lot to process while you were pretty much full bandwidth, just keeping the car on track and watching the mirrors and watching ahead."

[Article continues below]

Stella's 'very, very clear' appraisal

Whilst Norris and Piastri have always enjoyed a strong relationship, publicly at least, things have not always been as harmonious on track.

As recently as the Singapore Grand Prix, the pair clashed when they collided on the final lap of the sprint, throwing away valuable points in the team's bid to secure third in the F1 constructors' standings.

Having endured a tense title fight together last year, Stella believes the partnership is better because of it, although he was quick to acknowledge the work that has gone into getting them there.

"Therefore, I would like to praise definitely very, very clearly that this is one of the best races for Oscar and Lando," he said. "And when it comes to racing each other, you will have heard that we needed to help our drivers make sure they remember that when the car is your team-mate, you need to use extra care.

"This is a process that, for us, has been going on for some time now," he added. "We don't have to forget that we come from a season in which we have had Oscar and Lando fighting [for the title] until the last corner, and if anything, their relationship has improved after 2025.

"So we are on a journey, but you never have to consider that the job is done. Always keep lots of attention, conversations, and focus on this kind of matter. It's a really difficult one."

title: Charles Leclerc chastised for 'losing' Ferrari to Lewis Hamilton
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has been criticised by Jacques Villeneuve for allowing Lewis Hamilton to make Ferrari "his own" after joining the Scuderia last season.

Hamilton struggled to match Leclerc's levels of performance when he first joined the Italian team, but has been the stronger of the pairing this campaign.

But the British driver's relative lack of form was inconsequential as he was "very busy" putting his mark on the Maranello-based squad, according to the 1997 F1 drivers' champion.

Now, with the two drivers clashing on track and internal tensions rising, Villeneuve feels Hamilton has wrestled control of a team Leclerc has been the de facto leader of since he outmatched Sebastian Vettel upon arrival in 2019.

"If you look at it, last year Lewis was very busy making the team his own; that's what he was working on," the Canadian said on Sky Sports F1. "Not being quick, making sure that Ferrari would be his team."

Put to him that it is comparable to what Michael Schumacher did when he joined the Scuderia, Villeneuve continued: "Exactly, and Charles had how many years to do that? He didn't.

"He should never have lost that leadership, which means he never really had it.

"And Lewis, with all the championships he has, if he comes in and he just works on it a little bit, of course he'll move you away. It's natural."

[Article continues below]

Why Hamilton cannot be granted number 1 status

The Ferrari team-mates have clashed on track multiple times in recent rounds, and their relationship appears to be growing ever more fractured as a result.

Following the first incident at the Mexico City Grand Prix and some choice words said by both — and team principal Fred Vasseur in the aftermath — they have been trying to get back on the same page and present a united front.

That picture was shattered this weekend in Las Vegas when they collided during the 50-lap race, despite talks between them at the previous round in São Paulo.

It has led to questions about team orders and rules of engagement being asked, and some, like Villeneuve's former Williams team-mate Damon Hill, have gone as far as to suggest Hamilton should be granted priority over Leclerc.

Asked whether the seven-time F1 drivers' champion should be given number 1 status with full effort put behind him, Villeneuve highlighted the 41-year-old's titles.

He said: "They can't, because of the contract situation; we don't know what kind of contract Leclerc has. And obviously, he cannot be told [what to do].

"But if there's one of the two drivers knows how to win championships, it's Lewis, obviously."

title: Devastated Arvid Lindblad reveals 'very strange' problem after costly mistake
excerpt:
Arvid Lindblad has explained a "very strange feeling" he experienced in the moments leading up to his race-ending spin at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Lindblad was running an exceptional sixth place when he dropped his Racing Bulls behind the safety car on Lap 20 whilst trying to get heat into his cold tyres.

The Racing Bulls driver was unable to get going, and had to retire from the 50-lap grand prix in Sin City.

Reflecting on the error to media, including RacingNews365, a downtrodden Lindblad said: "I honestly don't know what happened.

"I had a very bad shift, but in the end, it is still my fault; there is no point in blaming that, but it was a very strange feeling and something I've not really experienced in the car.

"I wasn't doing anything strange; I was very slowly going on throttle, and then I was facing the wall.

"In the end, it's my fault, and I'll take it on the chin. But I can't sit here now and say I understand why, because it was the strangest thing I've experienced."
