title: Red Bull raise deliberate Max Verstappen scheme in 'breathtaking' Las Vegas win
excerpt:
Red Bull Laurent Mekies believes Max Verstappen was losing the lead "on purpose" during the Las Vegas Grand Prix to learn about the crucial run to the line.

In a grand prix dominated by the slipstream and tow effect, Verstappen was leading onto the Strip for most of the 50 laps and was passed by the likes of George Russell and Lando Norris during the slipstream fest into Turn 14 at the end of the long straight.

However, this then gave Verstappen the opportunity to be the car behind on the long blast from the final chicane, through the fast-left kink of the final corner and into Turn 1.

The Dutch driver quickly cottoned onto the fact that the race would ultimately be decided on the final lap blast from the chicane to the line, and asked his team if there were any other energy management settings he could use to ensure he was in a prime position to be behind coming off the Strip on the final lap.

As it turned out, Russell hit the barrier on Lap 48 of 50 when trying to pass Kimi Antonelli to get into second, with the world champion then suffering a de-rate starting the final lap which meant Verstappen was relatively untroubled, taking the flag 0.6s ahead of Lando Norris.

Reflecting, Mekies was of strong praise for the defensive masterclass Verstappen had put in, and how he allowed himself to be overtaken on purpose for the benefit of gathering knowledge for later in the race.

"I think Max clearly outsmarted the opposition today in the way he managed to defend for 50 laps," Mekies told media, including RacingNews365.

"Yes, he was overtaken a few times, and I think he probably did that on purpose a few times, and he probably explored every possible way around between the second-to-last and the last corner to the line.

"[This was] to the extent that he asked us to have another look at the scenario for the final lap, and obviously the guys were thinking about that as well for quite a while.

"The conclusions when we came back to him were that he was already mastering it and had explored all the options, so we felt he knew exactly what to do at that moment, and it proved to be the case.

"So he's done another outstanding race, an exceptional race, and I don't know if it is funny more than other ones, but it was breathtaking the way he resisted the pressure for so long."

[Article continues below]

Learnings for Red Bull

In the early part of the season, Red Bull struggled on energy-starved tracks such as Las Vegas, but owing to the high slipstream effect in Sin City, Mekies felt the team were unable to gain much knowledge about the strengths and weaknesses of its RB22 package.

"When it comes to energy-poor tracks, given how the race panned out with the extremely high slipstream effect, I think it is difficult to have a [picture]," he said.

"I would have loved to leave here with clear pictures of the pace of the car in the race against the opposition, but I think nobody has any real conclusions on that."

title: Fred Vasseur reveals 'what comes next' after latest Hamilton-Leclerc meltdown
excerpt:
Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur is planning further talks with his feuding drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc after their latest collision.

Speaking further about the discussion with Leclerc immediately after the race, Vasseur indicated that it was a rather one-way discussion.

"It was not a discussion. I spoke, and I think he apologised, that he understands blah blah blah, but the result is there: that he made a mistake."

"It is not an issue between Lewis and Fred or Charles and Fred. It is an issue between a team and two drivers.

"Honestly, it is not a matter of rules; it is not a matter of what you can do differently, except that you have to respect your team-mate.

title: George Russell takes full responsibility after race-wrecking Las Vegas error

title: Charles Leclerc reveals Ferrari summons message after Lewis Hamilton collision
excerpt:

The FIA stewards handed Leclerc a 10-second time penalty, ruling that he had started his move from too far back and had not earned the right to the corner. Leclerc eventually finished 10th, with Hamilton recovering to seventh.

It cost the Scuderia a potential podium, but certainly a significantly greater haul of points just a matter of weeks after the duo clashed in Mexico City.

Speaking to Viaplay after the race, Leclerc was asked what Vasseur had said to him.

"I don't feel it's very different compared to the wheel-to-wheel clashes we've had in the past, and I don't think there was any overdriving there whatsoever. Just by the situation that Lewis had with the McLaren in front, there was a natural opportunity for me to be down the inside there.

Leclerc set for Las Vegas personal reflection

Asked what needed to change following the incident, Leclerc was reluctant to go into detail about what had passed between himself and Vasseur.

"At the end of the day, I think the result is that today, because of something I did, we don't score the points that we should have, and that is not acceptable.

"I will look back at the incident and try to understand what I could have done better, differently, and to make sure that I don't ever find myself in this situation again. That's all I can say."
